final_note: You worked through D4.3 Climate change — 12 guide statements.

concepts.def: Change in the Earth's climate caused by human activity, in particular the warming that results from anthropogenic increases in the atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases. The IB limits the causes studied to carbon dioxide and methane, whose concentrations have risen since pre-industrial times because of human activities.

concepts.term: Anthropogenic sources of carbon dioxide and methane
concepts.def: Carbon dioxide concentration has risen (from about 280 ppm before industrialization to over 420 ppm) mainly through combustion of fossil fuels, deforestation and other land-use change, and cement production. Methane concentration has more than doubled mainly through enteric fermentation in ruminant livestock, rice paddies, landfill sites and leakage during the extraction and transport of fossil fuels. Both gases absorb long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth's surface, so their increase enhances the greenhouse effect.

A correlation is a relationship between two variables. In a positive correlation, higher values of one variable are associated with higher values of the other; in a negative correlation, higher values of one variable are associated with lower values of the other. Antarctic ice cores show a positive correlation between global temperature and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration over hundreds of thousands of years.

A correlation between two variables does not by itself show that one causes the other: both could be affected by a third factor, or the causal direction could be the reverse. The ice-core correlation between carbon dioxide and temperature does not prove that carbon dioxide raises global temperature; the causal link is established by other evidence, including laboratory measurements of the absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide and the physics of the greenhouse effect.

A cycle in which the consequence of a change increases the original change, moving the system further from its starting state. In global warming, warming triggers processes that release more greenhouse gases or increase the absorption of solar radiation, which causes further warming. Examples are release of carbon dioxide from the deep ocean, loss of reflective snow and ice, accelerated decomposition of peat and previously undecomposed organic matter in permafrost, release of methane from melting permafrost, and increases in droughts and forest fires.

The fraction of incoming solar radiation that a surface reflects. Snow and ice have a high albedo and reflect most of the solar radiation reaching them, whereas open water and bare ground have a low albedo and absorb most of it. Loss of snow and ice therefore increases the absorption of solar radiation, warming the surface and melting more snow and ice: a positive feedback.

Ground that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years, found across large areas of the Arctic and sub-Arctic. It contains vast quantities of organic matter that has accumulated without decomposing because it is frozen. When permafrost thaws, decomposers become active: aerobic decomposition releases carbon dioxide and anaerobic decomposition by methanogenic archaea in waterlogged thawed ground releases methane, both of which cause further warming.

concepts.term: Drought, forest fire and peat decomposition as positive feedbacks
concepts.def: Warming increases evaporation and the frequency of droughts, and drier vegetation and soil make forest fires more frequent and intense; fires release carbon dioxide from biomass and soil organic matter, causing further warming and more drought. Warming and drying of peat, and thawing of permafrost, also speed up decomposition of organic matter that had accumulated undecomposed, releasing carbon dioxide (and methane where the ground is waterlogged), which causes further warming.

A threshold beyond which a small further change causes an ecosystem to shift abruptly to a different state, which may be difficult or impossible to reverse. The change of boreal forests from net carbon accumulation to net carbon loss is an example: once drought, browning and fire outweigh primary production, the forest switches from a carbon sink to a carbon source.

The coniferous forest biome of high northern latitudes, with long cold winters and short growing seasons. Boreal forests have historically accumulated carbon, storing much of it in thick soil organic layers. Warmer temperatures and decreased winter snowfall are increasing the incidence of drought, reducing primary production and causing forest browning and more frequent and more intense forest fires.

A decline in the greenness and productivity of forest vegetation, detected from satellite measurements and ground surveys, caused by drought stress, reduced growth, needle loss and tree death. Browning in the taiga indicates a reduction in primary production and therefore in the uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Carbon in the soil organic layer of a boreal forest that escaped combustion in previous fires and has accumulated over many fire cycles, so it is older than the trees now growing. In the past, most fires burnt only the carbon that had been fixed since the last fire. When fires become more frequent and intense, they burn deeper and combust this legacy carbon, releasing carbon that had been stored for centuries and contributing to the switch from net accumulation to net loss.

Sea ice that is attached to the coast, to the sea floor or to grounded icebergs, so that it does not drift with winds and currents. Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) breed on landfast ice around Antarctica through the winter; the ice must persist until the chicks fledge in December and January. Warming is causing landfast ice to break out earlier, before the chicks have grown waterproof adult plumage, and colonies have suffered breeding failure as a result.

Frozen sea water floating on the ocean surface. Arctic sea ice provides walruses (Odobenus rosmarus) with a resting platform over the shallow continental shelf, close to the sea-floor molluscs on which they feed. As summer sea ice retreats into deep water beyond the shelf, walruses must haul out on land in large, crowded groups and make longer journeys to their feeding grounds, so the loss of sea ice is a loss of habitat.

The rise of cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean to the sunlit surface, where the nutrients (such as nitrate and phosphate) allow high rates of phytoplankton production. Nutrients accumulate at depth because dead organic matter sinks and is decomposed there. Warmer, less dense surface water forms a stable layer over the colder water below, so changes in ocean currents and surface warming can reduce or prevent upwelling, lowering ocean primary production and the energy flow through marine food chains.

A change in the geographical area occupied by a species. As the climate warms, temperate species tend to shift poleward and upslope so that they remain within the range of temperatures they can tolerate. Evidence includes upslope shifts of montane bird species in New Guinea and the northward spread, with contraction at the southern edge of the range, of tree species in North America. For plants the shift occurs across generations, through seed dispersal and differential survival, not by movement of individuals.

The decrease in the pH of the oceans caused by the dissolving of additional atmospheric carbon dioxide. Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions; these react with carbonate ions, lowering the carbonate ion concentration. Seawater remains slightly alkaline (mean surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1) but the lower carbonate concentration suppresses calcification, so corals build their calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly.

The loss of colour by reef-building corals when, stressed by unusually high water temperature, they expel the mutualistic photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) living in their tissues. The coral is left alive but pale and deprived of most of its food supply; if the stress is prolonged the coral starves and dies, whereas if the water cools soon enough it can regain its algae and recover.

The breakdown of a coral reef ecosystem that follows the death of its corals. Corals build the three-dimensional structure that provides habitat, shelter and food for a very large number of fish and invertebrate species; when the corals die the structure erodes and most of these species are lost, so the whole ecosystem collapses rather than a single species.

The removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and its long-term storage in a carbon sink such as biomass, soil or peat. Afforestation, forest regeneration and restoration of peat-forming wetlands are approaches that use natural processes to sequester carbon, offsetting anthropogenic emissions.

The planting of trees on land that has not recently been forested, to create a new carbon sink. There is active scientific debate over whether plantations of fast-growing non-native tree species or rewilding with native species offer the best approach to carbon sequestration: plantations sequester carbon rapidly at first, but native woodland may store more carbon in the long term, including in soil, and supports greater biodiversity.

The regrowth of forest on land that was previously forested and has been cleared or degraded, either by natural regeneration from seeds and regrowth or with assistance. As the regenerating forest grows, carbon is sequestered in biomass and soil.

Partially decomposed plant material that accumulates in waterlogged soils, where the lack of oxygen inhibits the saprotrophs that would otherwise decompose it fully. Peat formation naturally occurs in temperate and boreal zones and also very rapidly in some tropical ecosystems. Peatlands store large amounts of carbon; drained peat decomposes and releases carbon dioxide, so restoring peat-forming wetlands by re-wetting them is an approach to carbon sequestration.

Research into the timing of biological events, such as flowering, budburst and bud set in deciduous trees, and bird migration and nesting, and into the variables that influence that timing. Photoperiod and temperature patterns are examples of variables that act as cues, and long-term phenological records show how the timing of events is changing as the climate warms.

The length of the daily period of light, which at a given latitude follows the same annual pattern every year because it depends on the Earth's orbit and not on the weather. Many organisms use photoperiod as a cue for the timing of biological events, for example bud set in deciduous trees in autumn and the migration of many bird species, so events cued by photoperiod do not advance when the climate warms.

The loss of the matching in time between interdependent biological events in different populations when climate change shifts one event but not the other. Within an ecosystem, temperature may be the cue in one population while photoperiod is the cue in another. In the Arctic, spring growth of the mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) is cued by temperature and so is occurring earlier, whereas migration of reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) to the calving grounds is cued by photoperiod and has not advanced, so calves are born after the peak in plant growth and have less nutritious food.

An example of disrupted synchrony in north European forests: the peak biomass of the caterpillars that great tits (Parus major) feed to their nestlings has advanced with warmer springs, while the birds' egg-laying date has advanced less, so chicks hatch after the food peak and fewer survive. (Reported as removed from the 2028 guide; examined in 2026 and 2027.)

The number of generations an insect completes in a year. Insects are ectotherms whose development rate rises with temperature, so warmer springs and summers allow more generations to be completed. The spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus or Dendroctonus micans) has one generation per year in cool conditions but two or more in warm ones, so climate change increases beetle populations and the damage to spruce forests.

The relative contribution of an individual of a particular genotype or phenotype to the next generation, through survival and reproduction. Climate change alters which phenotypes have the highest fitness: in tawny owls (Strix aluco) the brown colour morph survives snowy winters less well than the grey morph, so as snow cover has decreased the fitness of the brown morph has risen relative to the grey morph.

mcqs.q: Antarctic ice cores show that, over the last 800 000 years, periods of high global temperature coincided with high atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations and periods of low temperature with low concentrations. Which statement about this evidence is correct?
options: It shows a positive correlation, but the causal link between carbon dioxide and temperature is established by other evidence.
It shows a positive correlation, which by itself proves that carbon dioxide raises global temperatures.
It shows a negative correlation in cold periods, when both variables fell, and a positive one in warm periods.
It shows a correlation, but the warming was caused by thinning of the ozone layer rather than by carbon dioxide.
mcqs.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: The ice-core data show a positive correlation over hundreds of thousands of years. A correlation does not prove causation; the causal link is confirmed by other evidence, such as the measured absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide.
rationales: The ice-core data show a positive correlation over hundreds of thousands of years. A correlation does not prove causation; the causal link is confirmed by other evidence, such as the measured absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide.

A student who takes a strong correlation as proof of cause picks this. Correlation alone cannot prove causation, since both variables could respond to a third factor; the causal link needs other evidence.

A student who thinks the sign of a correlation describes whether the variables are rising or falling picks this. High goes with high and low with low throughout, which is a single positive correlation.
A student who merges ozone depletion with global warming picks this. Ozone depletion is a separate problem; the causal link between carbon dioxide and warming is established by other evidence.

mcqs.q: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?
options: Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations
Escape of ancient methane trapped in bubbles in melting polar ice
mcqs.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly. Rice paddies, landfill and leakage from fossil fuel extraction are other anthropogenic sources.
rationales: A student who thinks population growth raises greenhouse gases through breathing picks this. Exhaled gases return carbon recently fixed by photosynthesis and are not a source of methane.

Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly. Rice paddies, landfill and leakage from fossil fuel extraction are other anthropogenic sources.
A student who assumes every greenhouse gas is a combustion product picks this. Complete combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide; methane is itself a fuel that combustion consumes.

A student who pictures greenhouse gas as ancient bubbles trapped in ice picks this. Ice sheets are not a store of methane, and the anthropogenic rise comes from enteric fermentation in livestock, rice paddies, landfill and leakage of natural gas during fossil fuel extraction and transport.

mcqs.q: In a data set of 40 countries, the higher the percentage of electricity generated by burning coal, the higher the carbon dioxide emissions per person. In the same countries, the greater the percentage of land covered by forest, the lower the net carbon dioxide emissions. Based on these data alone, how should the two relationships be described?
options: The first is a positive correlation and the second is a positive correlation too
The first is a strong correlation and the second is a much weaker correlation
The first is a positive correlation and the second is a negative correlation
The first is a causal relationship and the second is a negative correlation
mcqs.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: In the first, higher coal use goes with higher emissions: positive. In the second, higher forest cover goes with lower emissions: negative. Both are correlations; neither by itself proves causation.
rationales: A student who thinks a correlation is positive whenever a variable increases picks this. In the second relationship higher forest cover goes with lower emissions, which is a negative correlation.
A student who reads 'negative' as 'weak' picks this. The sign of a correlation is its direction, not its strength; nothing in the data says the second relationship is weaker.
In the first, higher coal use goes with higher emissions: positive. In the second, higher forest cover goes with lower emissions: negative. Both are correlations; neither by itself proves causation.
A student who takes a correlation as proof of cause picks this. Coal burning is known from other evidence to release carbon dioxide, but these data alone show a correlation, not causation.

mcqs.q: Which process is part of a positive feedback cycle that increases global warming?
options: More evaporation forms clouds that reflect sunlight and cool the surface
Melting snow and ice absorb heat from their surroundings and cool the oceans
Warming ocean water dissolves more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
Thawing permafrost releases methane gas into the atmosphere
mcqs.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
mcqs.explain: Methane is released from melting permafrost as previously frozen organic matter decomposes anaerobically. Methane is a greenhouse gas, so this causes further warming and further thawing: a positive feedback cycle.
rationales: A student who thinks positive feedback restores the original state picks a stabilizing process. This would be negative feedback; positive feedback amplifies the warming.
A student who thinks of ice cooling a drink picks this. The important effect of losing snow and ice is the loss of a reflective surface, which increases absorption of solar radiation.
A student who generalizes from the solubility of solids picks this. Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so warming oceans release carbon dioxide.

Methane is released from melting permafrost as previously frozen organic matter decomposes anaerobically. Methane is a greenhouse gas, so this causes further warming and further thawing: a positive feedback cycle.

mcqs.q: As the oceans warm, the amount of carbon dioxide that stays dissolved in the deep ocean changes. Why does this act as a positive feedback in global warming?
options: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so the warming ocean releases carbon dioxide, which enhances the greenhouse effect and warms the ocean further.
Gases are more soluble in warmer water, so the ocean takes up carbon dioxide and this stored gas traps heat in the water, warming it further.
The carbon dioxide released returns the atmospheric concentration to its earlier value, which brings the temperature back to normal.
Warming melts the sea ice, which releases ancient carbon dioxide that had been trapped as bubbles inside the ice since it formed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
mcqs.explain: The solubility of a gas falls as temperature rises. Carbon dioxide released from the deep ocean adds to the atmospheric concentration, increasing the greenhouse effect and causing more warming, which releases more carbon dioxide.
rationales: The solubility of a gas falls as temperature rises. Carbon dioxide released from the deep ocean adds to the atmospheric concentration, increasing the greenhouse effect and causing more warming, which releases more carbon dioxide.
A student who assumes warm water dissolves more, as it does for sugar, picks this. Gases become less soluble as temperature rises, so the ocean releases carbon dioxide rather than absorbing more.
A student who thinks positive feedback restores a system picks this. That would be negative feedback; here the release adds carbon dioxide and pushes the temperature further from its original value.
A student who pictures trapped bubbles of ancient gas picks this. The feedback comes from the reduced solubility of carbon dioxide in warmer water, not from gas trapped in ice.

mcqs.q: Fresh snow reflects about 85% of the solar radiation reaching it, whereas open ocean water reflects about 7%. Since 1980 the area of the Arctic Ocean covered by sea ice in September has fallen by more than 40%. What is the most likely consequence for the Arctic climate?
options: Melting ice takes in heat from the water, so the Arctic Ocean is cooled and further loss of ice is slowed down.
The exposed dark water absorbs far more of the solar radiation, warming the region and melting still more ice.
The extra open water evaporates, and the cloud that forms reflects radiation and restores the ice cover.
Sea level rises as the ice melts and floods the coasts, but the amount of radiation absorbed is unchanged.
mcqs.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
mcqs.explain: Open water reflects only about 7% of solar radiation and absorbs the rest, whereas snow-covered ice reflects most of it. Loss of ice therefore increases absorption and warming, which melts more ice: a positive feedback cycle.
rationales: A student who applies the ice-in-a-drink idea picks this. The dominant effect is that the exposed dark water absorbs far more solar radiation than the ice did, warming the region.

Open water reflects only about 7% of solar radiation and absorbs the rest, whereas snow-covered ice reflects most of it. Loss of ice therefore increases absorption and warming, which melts more ice: a positive feedback cycle.
A student who expects feedback to restore the original state picks this. The loss of a reflective surface amplifies warming; it is a positive feedback, not a self-correcting one.
A student who thinks melting sea ice raises sea level picks this. Floating ice displaces its own mass of water, so sea level hardly changes, and the absorption of radiation changes greatly.

mcqs.q: Which sequence of events explains how boreal forests in a warming climate change from net carbon accumulation to net carbon loss?
options: Warmer conditions and more carbon dioxide speed up photosynthesis, producing more litter, so decomposition releases more carbon than the trees fix.
More frequent fires burn the trees, but regrowth reabsorbs that carbon, so the net loss comes only from timber removed by logging.
Warming and less winter snow cause drought, reduced primary production, forest browning and more fires that burn legacy carbon.
The forest passes a tipping point at which warming stops, and its carbon balance then slowly returns to what it was before.
mcqs.specStatementText: Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source
mcqs.explain: Reduced snowfall and warmer temperatures leave the soil drier, so drought reduces primary production, causes browning and makes fires more frequent and intense. Fires that combust legacy carbon release more carbon than the forest fixes.
rationales: A student who expects warmth and carbon dioxide to boost growth picks this. In the taiga, warming brings drought, and primary production falls rather than rising.
A student who thinks fires are carbon neutral picks this. Intense fires combust legacy carbon from the soil organic layer, which regrowth does not replace before the next fire.

Reduced snowfall and warmer temperatures leave the soil drier, so drought reduces primary production, causes browning and makes fires more frequent and intense. Fires that combust legacy carbon release more carbon than the forest fixes.

A student who thinks a tipping point is a gradual, reversible turning point picks this. A tipping point is a threshold beyond which the forest shifts to a new state, net carbon loss, that may not reverse.

mcqs.q: Researchers measured the carbon in the soil organic layer of a boreal forest after fires. In stands older than 70 years, the carbon that remained was older than the trees and had survived earlier fires. In stands younger than 60 years on drier sites, the fire had burnt through this old carbon. What do these results show?
options: Fires release only carbon fixed since the previous fire, so regrowth of the trees will restore the carbon balance.
The forest has crossed a tipping point, so its carbon stock will recover gradually once the fires are out.
The old carbon lost from the young stands was ancient gas trapped in frozen soil that escaped as it thawed.
Fires in young stands on dry sites combust legacy carbon that older stands protect from burning.
mcqs.specStatementText: Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source
mcqs.explain: Legacy carbon is carbon in the soil organic layer that survived previous fires. In older stands a thick organic layer protected it, but in young stands on dry sites the fire burnt into it, releasing carbon stored over many fire cycles.
rationales: A student who thinks fires are carbon neutral picks this. In the young stands the fire burnt carbon older than the trees, so it released carbon that regrowth cannot replace before the next fire.
A student who thinks a tipping point is followed by gradual recovery picks this. A tipping point marks a shift to a new state, net carbon loss, which may not be reversible.
A student who pictures trapped gas picks this. The old carbon was stored organic matter in the soil organic layer that was combusted by the fire, not gas released by thawing.

Legacy carbon is carbon in the soil organic layer that survived previous fires. In older stands a thick organic layer protected it, but in young stands on dry sites the fire burnt into it, releasing carbon stored over many fire cycles.

mcqs.q: Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) breed on landfast ice during the Antarctic winter, and the chicks fledge in December and January. Why does the early breakout of landfast ice threaten breeding?
options: If the ice breaks out before the chicks have grown waterproof adult plumage, they fall into the sea and drown or die of cold.
The open water exposes the penguins to warmer air, which they cannot tolerate because they are adapted to cold.
The melting ice raises the sea level and floods the colony on the shore where the eggs are being incubated.
Walruses that share the ice platform crowd onto the remaining ice and trample the eggs and chicks.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polar ice as habitat: emperor penguins and walruses
mcqs.explain: Landfast ice must persist until the chicks fledge. When it breaks out early, chicks that still have down rather than waterproof feathers are lost to the sea, and colonies can suffer near-total breeding failure.
rationales: Landfast ice must persist until the chicks fledge. When it breaks out early, chicks that still have down rather than waterproof feathers are lost to the sea, and colonies can suffer near-total breeding failure.
A student who thinks polar animals are threatened by heat itself picks this. The threat is the loss of the ice platform on which the chicks are reared, not the temperature.
A student who thinks melting sea ice raises sea level picks this. Floating ice does not raise sea level, and the eggs are incubated on the ice itself, not on the shore.
A student who mixes up the faunas of the two poles picks this. Walruses live in the Arctic; emperor penguins breed in the Antarctic, where there are no walruses.

mcqs.q: Walruses (Odobenus rosmarus) feed on molluscs on the floor of the shallow Arctic continental shelf and rest on sea ice between dives. Summer sea ice now retreats into deep water beyond the shelf. What is the consequence for the walruses?
options: They overheat in the warmer water, because their thick blubber prevents them from losing heat quickly enough to survive.
They must haul out on land in large crowded groups and travel much further to reach their feeding grounds.
They move to the Antarctic, where the landfast ice still provides a resting platform close to the shelf.
Sea level rises as the ice melts, so the shelf becomes too deep for them to reach the sea floor.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polar ice as habitat: emperor penguins and walruses
mcqs.explain: With no sea ice over the shallow shelf, walruses rest on beaches in crowds of thousands, where calves can be trampled, and must swim long distances to feed. The sea ice was their habitat and it has been lost.
rationales: A student who thinks the threat from warming is heat stress picks this. The problem is the loss of a resting platform near the feeding grounds, not the water temperature.

With no sea ice over the shallow shelf, walruses rest on beaches in crowds of thousands, where calves can be trampled, and must swim long distances to feed. The sea ice was their habitat and it has been lost.
A student who treats the two poles as one place picks this. Walruses are Arctic animals and do not occur in the Antarctic.
A student who thinks melting sea ice raises sea level picks this. Floating ice does not raise sea level; the problem is that the ice has moved away from the shallow shelf.

mcqs.q: Off the coast of Peru, cold nutrient-rich water normally rises to the surface. In some years the surface water is unusually warm, and the catch of anchovies falls sharply. Which explanation is correct?
options: Warm surface water raises the rate of enzyme activity in phytoplankton, which grow so fast that they use up all the oxygen the anchovies need.
Phytoplankton obtain their nutrients from sunlight, so the fall in the catch must be caused by the greater cloud cover in the warmer years.
Warm surface water is less dense and does not mix with the water below, so fewer nutrients reach the surface and primary production falls.
Warm water dissolves more carbon dioxide, which acidifies the sea and kills the eggs and larvae of the anchovies.
mcqs.specStatementText: Warm surface water blocks nutrient upwelling
mcqs.explain: Warm surface water forms a stable layer that prevents nutrient upwelling. Ocean primary production falls, so less energy flows through the food chain to the anchovies and the catch collapses.
rationales: A student who applies the enzyme–temperature rule to the whole ocean picks this. Production falls in warm years because nutrients, not temperature, limit phytoplankton, and fewer nutrients reach the surface.
A student who thinks sunlight supplies nutrients picks this. Light supplies energy; the mineral nutrients that limit phytoplankton come from below, and the warm water stops them rising.
Warm surface water forms a stable layer that prevents nutrient upwelling. Ocean primary production falls, so less energy flows through the food chain to the anchovies and the catch collapses.
A student who thinks warm water dissolves more gas picks this. Warmer water dissolves less carbon dioxide; the collapse is due to the loss of nutrient upwelling and primary production.

mcqs.q: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?
options: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.
The correlation between warming and the shift proves that no other factor was involved.
The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.
mcqs.specStatementText: Species move poleward and upslope
mcqs.explain: Both range limits moving upslope as the region warmed is the pattern expected when a species tracks the band of temperatures it can tolerate. Upslope shifts of montane birds in New Guinea are evidence of range shifts driven by climate change.
rationales: A student who equates a range shift with expansion picks this. Both limits moved up by a similar amount, so the range moved rather than growing.

A student who thinks a range shift is cost-free picks this. A mountain narrows towards its summit, so a band of the same height contains less area higher up, and species near the top have nowhere left to go.
A student who treats a correlation as proof of cause picks this. The pattern is consistent with warming, but a correlation alone cannot rule out other factors.

Both range limits moving upslope as the region warmed is the pattern expected when a species tracks the band of temperatures it can tolerate. Upslope shifts of montane birds in New Guinea are evidence of range shifts driven by climate change.

mcqs.q: In a survey of forests in the eastern United States, seedlings of several northern tree species were found on average further north than mature trees of the same species, while at the southern edge of the range there were mature trees but few seedlings. What does this indicate?
options: The ranges are shifting northward, with seedlings establishing beyond the northern edge and the range contracting at the southern edge.
The mature trees are themselves migrating northward as individuals, leaving the southern part of their range behind them.
The species are expanding their ranges, since seedlings are appearing in the north while mature trees remain in the south.
The species are unaffected by warming, because trees of some age are still present right across the whole of the range.
mcqs.specStatementText: Species move poleward and upslope
mcqs.explain: Trees shift range across generations. Seeds that establish north of the current adults extend the range northward, and failure of seedlings in the south means the southern edge will retreat as the mature trees die: northward spread with range contraction.
rationales: Trees shift range across generations. Seeds that establish north of the current adults extend the range northward, and failure of seedlings in the south means the southern edge will retreat as the mature trees die: northward spread with range contraction.
A student who pictures a range shift as individuals moving picks this. Rooted trees cannot move; the shift happens through seed dispersal and the survival of seedlings over generations.
A student who reads any shift as expansion picks this. Few seedlings in the south means that edge will not be replaced when the adults die, so the range contracts there.
A student who thinks species simply move with the climate unharmed picks this. The lack of regeneration in the south shows the range is being lost there.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly matches a threat to coral reefs with its cause?
options: Coral bleaching is caused by ocean acidification, which dissolves the pigments out of the coral tissue.
Suppression of calcification in corals is caused by the increased carbon dioxide concentration of seawater.
Ocean acidification lowers the pH of seawater below 7, so the calcium carbonate skeletons of corals dissolve away.
Coral bleaching kills the polyps immediately, so a reef that has bleached can no longer recover.
mcqs.specStatementText: Coral reefs: acidification and bleaching
mcqs.explain: Extra dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the pH and the carbonate ion concentration of seawater, so corals build their calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly.
rationales: A student who merges the two threats picks this. Bleaching is caused by increased water temperature, which makes corals expel their zooxanthellae; acidification suppresses calcification.
Extra dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the pH and the carbonate ion concentration of seawater, so corals build their calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly.
A student who reads acidification as 'becoming acidic' picks this. Seawater remains alkaline at about pH 8.1; the harm is a reduced carbonate concentration that suppresses calcification.
A student who thinks white coral is dead coral picks this. A bleached coral is alive; it dies only if the heat stress is prolonged, and can otherwise regain its algae.

mcqs.q: During a marine heatwave, the corals on a reef turned white. When the water cooled four weeks later, most of the corals regained their colour. Which explanation is correct?
options: The corals died when they turned white, and the colour came from new corals that settled on the skeletons within four weeks.
The warm water became acidic and bleached the pigments, which re-formed once the pH returned to normal.
Heat stress made the corals expel their zooxanthellae, and they took the algae up again once the stress had ended.
The pH of the seawater fell below 7 in the heat and dissolved the skeletons, which were rebuilt when it rose again.
mcqs.specStatementText: Coral reefs: acidification and bleaching
mcqs.explain: High temperature causes corals to expel their mutualistic algae, leaving the white skeleton visible through the tissue. The corals stayed alive, and once the water cooled they regained their algae and their colour.
rationales: A student who thinks bleached coral is dead picks this. New corals could not grow to cover a reef in four weeks; the original corals were alive and recovered their algae.
A student who thinks acidification causes bleaching picks this. Bleaching is a response to heat stress; the colour is lost with the expelled algae, not chemically bleached.

High temperature causes corals to expel their mutualistic algae, leaving the white skeleton visible through the tissue. The corals stayed alive, and once the water cooled they regained their algae and their colour.
A student who thinks the sea becomes acidic picks this. Seawater stays alkaline, and skeletons could not be dissolved and rebuilt in weeks; the corals had lost and regained their algae.

mcqs.q: A drained peatland that had been releasing carbon dioxide is re-wetted so that the soil becomes waterlogged again. Why does this restoration act as an approach to carbon sequestration?
options: Waterlogging speeds up rotting, so plant remains turn into peat faster and store carbon
The cold of the water stops decomposition, so the carbon in plant remains stays stored
The weight of the water compresses the dead plants into peat, locking the carbon in
Without oxygen, saprotrophs cannot decompose plant remains, which build up as peat
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
mcqs.explain: Saprotrophs need oxygen for aerobic respiration. Re-wetting makes the soil anaerobic again, so the decomposition that was releasing carbon dioxide from the drained peat is inhibited and partially decomposed plant material once more accumulates as peat, storing carbon.
rationales: A student who expects wet things to rot faster picks this. Waterlogging excludes oxygen and so inhibits the saprotrophs; peat is plant material that has not fully decomposed, and it stores carbon because decomposition is slowed, not speeded up.

A student who thinks peat is a cold-climate product picks this. Peat forms very rapidly in some warm tropical ecosystems; it is the lack of oxygen in waterlogged soil, not cold, that inhibits decomposition and lets carbon accumulate.

A student who models peat on coal formation picks this. Peat accumulates at the surface of waterlogged soil because decomposition is inhibited; compression is not what forms it or what stores the carbon.

Saprotrophs need oxygen for aerobic respiration. Re-wetting makes the soil anaerobic again, so the decomposition that was releasing carbon dioxide from the drained peat is inhibited and partially decomposed plant material once more accumulates as peat, storing carbon.

mcqs.q: A government wants to sequester carbon on degraded land. Option A is a plantation of a fast-growing non-native conifer, harvested every 40 years. Option B is to allow native woodland to regenerate naturally. Scientists disagree about which is better. Which statement about this debate is justified?
options: The plantation sequesters carbon faster at first, but native woodland may store more in the long term, so the evidence does not settle the question.
The plantation is certainly better, because the fastest rate of tree growth gives the greatest amount of carbon sequestered.
Both options lock the carbon away permanently once the trees grow, so the only real difference between them is the cost.
Both options are afforestation and involve growing trees on the land, so they will sequester the same amount of carbon.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
mcqs.explain: This is the active scientific debate the IB refers to. Fast-growing plantations give rapid early sequestration; native regeneration is slower but may store more carbon over the long term, including in soil, and has other benefits. Neither is established as best.
rationales: This is the active scientific debate the IB refers to. Fast-growing plantations give rapid early sequestration; native regeneration is slower but may store more carbon over the long term, including in soil, and has other benefits. Neither is established as best.
A student who reasons from growth rate alone, and assumes the question is settled, picks this. Harvesting, soil carbon and long-term storage all matter, and scientists actively disagree.
A student who thinks carbon taken up by trees is stored for ever picks this. Harvested timber, decomposition and fire return carbon to the atmosphere, which is central to the debate.

A student who treats all tree-based approaches as the same picks this. Option A is afforestation with a plantation; option B is forest regeneration, and the two differ in species, harvesting and long-term storage.

mcqs.q: Which statement about phenology is correct?
options: It investigates how the environment alters the phenotype of an organism during its lifetime.
It investigates the timing of biological events such as budburst, flowering and migration.
It shows that temperature is the cue for every seasonal event in every species.
It shows that the photoperiod at a given latitude has changed as the climate warms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phenology: what sets the timing of the seasons' events
mcqs.explain: Phenology is research into the timing of biological events and the variables, such as photoperiod and temperature patterns, that influence that timing.
rationales: A student who confuses phenology with phenotype picks this. Phenology is research into the timing of biological events, not into how characteristics develop.
Phenology is research into the timing of biological events and the variables, such as photoperiod and temperature patterns, that influence that timing.
A student who assumes warmth drives all of spring picks this. Photoperiod is the main cue for some events, such as bud set and the migration of many birds.
A student who thinks longer days come earlier with warming picks this. Day length at a given latitude and date is fixed by the Earth's orbit and is unaffected by climate change.

mcqs.q: A migratory bird species arrives at its northern breeding grounds on almost the same date every year, whether the spring is warm or cold. In the same region, the date of budburst in birch trees varies by up to three weeks between years. What can be concluded about the cues?
options: Both are cued by temperature, but the birds respond to it much less strongly than the trees
Both are cued by photoperiod, which varies between years according to the spring weather
Migration is cued mainly by photoperiod, whereas budburst is cued mainly by temperature
Both respond to the same cue, so the timing of the two events will remain synchronized
mcqs.specStatementText: Phenology: what sets the timing of the seasons' events
mcqs.explain: Photoperiod is identical on the same date each year, so an event on a fixed date is consistent with a photoperiod cue. Budburst varies with the warmth of the spring, consistent with a temperature cue.
rationales: A student who assumes temperature cues everything picks this. A date that does not vary with the warmth of the spring points to a cue that does not vary between years: photoperiod.
A student who thinks day length changes with the weather picks this. Photoperiod on a given date is the same every year, which is why it cannot explain the varying budburst date.

Photoperiod is identical on the same date each year, so an event on a fixed date is consistent with a photoperiod cue. Budburst varies with the warmth of the spring, consistent with a temperature cue.
A student who thinks all species in an ecosystem shift together picks this. The two events already vary differently between years, so they are responding to different cues.

mcqs.q: In the Arctic, spring growth of the mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) is triggered by rising temperature, whereas the migration of reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) to their calving grounds is triggered by increasing day length. Springs are now warmer and earlier. What is the expected effect?
options: Both events advance by the same number of days, so synchrony between them is maintained
The reindeer switch to using temperature as their cue and arrive earlier to match the plants
Day length also increases earlier in a warm spring, so the reindeer migrate earlier as well
Peak plant growth occurs before the calves are born, so they have less food
mcqs.specStatementText: When the cues disagree, synchrony breaks
mcqs.explain: Plant growth, cued by temperature, now peaks earlier, but the reindeer, cued by photoperiod, arrive and calve on the same dates as before. The calves miss the most nutritious young growth, and calf survival falls: synchrony is disrupted.
rationales: A student who thinks all species shift together picks this. Only the temperature-cued event advances; the photoperiod-cued migration keeps to the same dates.
A student who expects organisms to adjust at will picks this. The cue a population uses is heritable; it does not change within a generation.
A student who thinks photoperiod shifts with the weather picks this. Day length on a given date is fixed by the Earth's orbit and does not change in a warm year.

Plant growth, cued by temperature, now peaks earlier, but the reindeer, cued by photoperiod, arrive and calve on the same dates as before. The calves miss the most nutritious young growth, and calf survival falls: synchrony is disrupted.

mcqs.q: The spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) completes one generation per year in cool summers but two or three in warm summers. In a region where mean summer temperature has risen by 2 °C, the area of spruce forest killed by the beetle has increased greatly. Which explanation is correct?
options: The number of generations per year is fixed genetically, so the extra damage must be due to beetles moving in from elsewhere.
Faster development at higher temperatures allows more generations per year, so beetle numbers build up more rapidly.
Adult beetles live longer in the warmth, so each one attacks more trees over the course of its lifetime.
Warmer conditions increase the growth of the spruce trees, and the beetles feed on this extra wood.
mcqs.specStatementText: More insect generations per year
mcqs.explain: Insects are ectotherms whose development speeds up as temperature rises. Extra generations within a year multiply the population, so more trees are attacked and killed.
rationales: A student who thinks life cycles per year are a fixed species characteristic picks this. Beetle development rate rises with temperature, so more generations are completed in warm years.
Insects are ectotherms whose development speeds up as temperature rises. Extra generations within a year multiply the population, so more trees are attacked and killed.
A student who confuses lifespan with generation time picks this. Warmth shortens the time from egg to adult; it is more generations, not longer-lived beetles, that raises numbers.
A student who assumes warmth benefits trees picks this. Warm, dry conditions stress spruce and weaken their resin defences; the damage rises because beetle populations grow.

mcqs.q: In Finland, tawny owls (Strix aluco) occur as a grey morph and a brown morph, and the colour is inherited. Brown owls survived snowy winters less well than grey owls. Between 1981 and 2008 winters became milder with less snow, and the proportion of brown owls rose from about 30% to about 50%. What best explains the change?
options: Individual grey owls gradually became browner over the years, as their plumage no longer needed to match snow in winter.
Mutations producing brown plumage occurred more often once the winter snow cover had gone from the region.
The fitness of the brown morph rose as snow cover fell, so brown alleles increased in frequency by natural selection.
The change is far too rapid to be evolution, so it must be a chance fluctuation in the numbers of each morph from year to year.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tawny owls: evolution within decades
mcqs.explain: With less snow, brown owls no longer suffered the higher winter mortality they had in snowy years, so they survived and reproduced better. Their allele became more common in the population: evolution as a consequence of climate change.
rationales: A student who thinks individuals adjust their colour to the environment picks this. Colour morph is inherited and fixed for life; the change is in the proportions of the two morphs in the population.
A student who thinks mutation responds to need picks this. Both alleles already existed; what changed was their relative fitness, and selection altered their frequencies.

With less snow, brown owls no longer suffered the higher winter mortality they had in snowy years, so they survived and reproduced better. Their allele became more common in the population: evolution as a consequence of climate change.

A student who thinks evolution needs millions of years picks this. A consistent rise over three decades, matching a heritable trait to a changed environment, is natural selection observed in real time.

mcqs.q: The proportion of brown tawny owls (Strix aluco) in a population has risen over three decades as winter snow cover has decreased. Which statement about this change is correct?
options: It is not evolution, because evolution takes many thousands of years to produce any change.
It is not evolution, because the individual owls changed their colour to suit the milder conditions.
It is evolution, because the reduced snow cover caused new mutations for brown plumage to arise.
It is evolution, because the frequency of the brown allele in the population has changed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tawny owls: evolution within decades
mcqs.explain: Evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics of a population. The rise of the brown morph is a change in allele frequency caused by natural selection under changed snow cover.
rationales: A student who links evolution only to the geological timescale picks this. Strong selection on a heritable trait changes allele frequencies within a few generations.
A student who attributes the change to individuals adapting picks this. Colour morph is inherited and does not change during an owl's life.
A student who thinks environmental change directs mutation picks this. The brown allele was already present; selection changed its frequency.
Evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics of a population. The rise of the brown morph is a change in allele frequency caused by natural selection under changed snow cover.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D4.3 Climate change

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only carbon dioxide and methane are treated as anthropogenic greenhouse gases. Nitrous oxide, water vapour, halocarbons and the ozone layer are not presented as causes of climate change (the ozone layer appears only inside a documented misconception, m03, and its distractors), and no radiative-forcing values or global warming potentials are used.
